newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Key political parties, leaders in Algeria's poll.
newsitem.headline: Key political parties, leaders in Algeria's poll.

text.p: Five parties have emerged from campaigning in Algeria to take dominant positions ahead of Thursday's parliamentary elections.
The ballot is the first since the nation's experiment with a multi-party general election was cancelled in 1992, bringing years of bloodshed.
Following are details of party plans and key people.
NATIONAL DEMOCRATIC RALLY (RND)

The RND, founded in early April, groups President Liamine Zeroual's core political supporters. Its platform is inspired largely by Zeroual's programme pledging to restore peace and stability, a cautious pace to privatising state-owned companies and a welfare scheme focusing on helping the poor affected by the economy's transition towards a free market.
The party is fielding candidates in all of Algeria's 48 constituencies and in six of the eight constituencies allotted to Algerian expatriates in Europe and elsewhere.

Algerian critics say the newly created RND showed the government's eagerness to firm up its own political base in the forthcoming parliament. The aim, those critics say, is to use the "democratic weapon" to shunt main legal opposition groups into the margins.
RND leaders say the party was created to fill a political void left by fractious opposition leaders who failed to answer mainstream Algerian needs.
Among the RND candidates standing for the 380-seat National Assembly election are Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia, other ministers and Zeroual's close aides, including former Prime Minister Mokdad Sifi.

The RND is headed by Abdelkader Bensalah, president of government-appointed Transitional National Council, a quasi-parliament. Bensalah, 56, was a Foreign Ministry spokesman in 1992 and is a former parliament deputy.
MOVEMENT OF A PEACEFUL SOCIETY (MPS)

Algeria's main legal Islamist party changed its name early in April to conform to a new law banning political parties based on Islam. The former Movement of the Islamic Society -- known by its Arabic acronym Hamas -- became Movement of a Peaceful Society, or MPS.
But the name change did not alter the group's core policies.

It is led by Mahfoud Nahnah, a telegenic and colourful former Arabic language teacher and imam. He has transformed from a radical Molsem fundamentalist firebrand in the 1980s into an "objective ally" of a government engaged in a battle against the radical Islamists.

Critics say Nahnah is engaged in "back-scratching" with the military which is trying to wipe out his bitter rivals in the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS). But his supporters brush aside the criticism, blaming Algeria's woes on the Moslem radicalism that Nahnah has denounced.
The party officially advocates "incremental change" through dialogue and participation in political life. It joined in Zeroual's government in 1995 filling two junior portfolios.

It advocates a leading role for the private sector in the economy, and focuses on promises to ease the plight of the jobless -- 2.5 million mainly young unemployed. It also says government must finance the construction of small housing units to help young people get married. Thousands of young Algerians are unable to marry because of the chronic housing shortage.

Nahnah, who won one-third of the 1995 vote that returned Zeroual to power, claims his party will gain a 40 percent vote share this time. MPS will field candidates in 52 of Algeria's 56 overall constituencies.
SOCIALIST FORCES FRONT (FFS)

FFS was created in 1963 in opposition to then president Ahmed Ben Bella's one-party rule. It draws its main support from the northeastern areas dominated by Algerian Berbers and middle-class urban residents in Algiers and some other cities.
The party will field candidates in 36 constituencies.

It insists that dialogue with the main opposition, including the FIS, is the only way out of Algeria's crisis. It advocates a moderate role for the government in the economy and a more even distribution of the nation's income.
RALLY FOR DEMOCRACY AND CULTURE (RCD)
The RCD was set up in 1989 by former FFS members. It is the staunchest backer of the military against Moslem rebels.

Its leader, Said Saadi, 50, won 10 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential poll. The RCD advocates a Turkish-style secular state, saying the politicisation of the Moslem faith has caused havoc in Algeria.
The party will field candidates in 38 constituencies. Its manifesto, "70 proposals for Algeria", promises more economic reform and a battle againist corruption and mismanagement.
NATIONAL LIBERATION FRONT (FLN)

The FLN is the founder of the Algerian nation, having led seven years of bloody war to end more than a century of French colonial rule in 1962. The party ruled Algeria until its grip in power was loosened by growing opposition and the dwindling value of oil and gas exports in the late 1980s.

It was humiliated in two successive elections in 1990 and 1991 at the hands of emerging radical Islamists. FLN joined the opposition camp early in 1992, attacking the authorities for scrapping a general poll in which Islamists were leading.
The party changed its leadership in 1995 and altered its policy hoping to get closer to Zeroual, but the move backfired after the president's supporters created RND and tried to woo voters from FLN.
Headed by former finance minister Boualem Benhamouda, FLN will field candidates in 54 constituencies and is promising voters stability and peace if they trust the party to lead Algeria again.
